Abstract:The dichromatic number $\vec\chi(D)$ of a digraph $D$ is the minimum size of a partition of its vertices into acyclic induced subgraphs. We denote by $\lambda(D)$ the maximum local edge connectivity of a digraph $D$. Neumann-Lara proved that for every digraph $D$, $\vec\chi(D) \leq \lambda(D) + 1$. In this paper, we characterize the digraphs $D$ for which $\vec\chi(D) = \lambda(D) + 1$. This generalizes an analogue result for undirected graph proved by Stiebitz and Toft as well as the directed version of Brooks' Theorem proved by Mohar. Along the way, we introduce a generalization of Hajós join that gives a new way to construct families of dicritical digraphs that is of independent interest.

# Partial structural attack on Conjecture 9.2

## 1. Setup

For a digraph \(D\), let \(B(D)\) be its **digon graph**: it is the undirected graph on \(V(D)\) in which \(xy\) is an edge exactly when both \(xy\) and \(yx\) are arcs of \(D\).

Write \(\overleftrightarrow{G}\) for the symmetric digraph obtained from an undirected graph \(G\).

The difficult direction of Conjecture 9.2 is

\[
D\text{ is 2-extremal}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D\in\mathcal H_2.
\]

The arguments below apply to a subdigraph-minimal digraph with

\[
\vec\chi(D)=3,\qquad \lambda(D)=2.
\]

Such a digraph will be called \(3\)-dicritical. This is the relevant critical object in the extremal-block reduction. For completeness, the following lemma justifies that reduction under the usual hypotheses on an extremal block.

---

## 2. Extremal blocks are critical

### Lemma 2.1
Let \(D\) be strong, let its underlying undirected graph be 2-connected, and suppose

\[
\vec\chi(D)=3,\qquad \lambda(D)\le 2.
\]

Then \(D\) is \(3\)-dicritical.

### Proof
Choose an inclusion-minimal subdigraph \(Q\subseteq D\) with \(\vec\chi(Q)=3\).

First, \(Q\) is strong: otherwise all directed cycles lie in its strong components, so one proper strong component would already have dichromatic number \(3\).

We claim that \(Q\) is 2-arc-strong. Suppose that a nonempty proper \(X\subset V(Q)\) satisfies \(d_Q^+(X)\le1\). The two proper subdigraphs \(Q[X]\) and \(Q[\overline X]\) have 2-dicolorings. If the unique arc from \(X\) to \(\overline X\) is \(xy\), permute the two colors on one side so that \(x\) and \(y\) receive different colors. Combining the colorings gives a 2-dicoloring of \(Q\): a monochromatic directed cycle crossing the cut would have to use \(xy\), which is bichromatic. This is a contradiction. Thus every nontrivial directed cut has size at least two, and directed Menger gives two arc-disjoint \(u\)-to-\(v\) paths for every ordered pair \(u\ne v\).

We use the following elementary ear fact.

> If \(H\) is a proper strong subdigraph of a strong digraph \(D\), and the underlying graph of \(D\) is 2-connected, then either \(D\) has an additional arc between two vertices of \(H\), or there is a directed path \(P\) with distinct endpoints in \(H\) and all internal vertices outside \(H\).

To verify this, take a weak component \(W\) of \(D-V(H)\). It has at least two distinct neighbours in \(H\), since otherwise its unique attachment would be a cutvertex of the underlying graph. Consider the condensation of \(D[W]\). Every source component receives an arc from \(H\), and every sink component sends an arc to \(H\). If no directed \(H\)-ear with distinct endpoints exists, label each condensation component by the unique vertex of \(H\) from which it is reachable through \(W\), equivalently the unique vertex of \(H\) reachable from it through \(W\). Labels agree along every condensation arc and hence throughout \(W\). All attachments of \(W\) would then use one vertex of \(H\), a contradiction.

If \(Q\ne D\), this ear fact gives either an extra arc \(xy\), or a directed \(Q\)-ear from \(x\) to \(y\), with \(x\ne y\). Together with two arc-disjoint \(x\)-to-\(y\) paths in \(Q\), this produces three arc-disjoint \(x\)-to-\(y\) paths in \(D\), contradicting \(\lambda(D)\le2\). Hence \(Q=D\). ∎

Thus it is legitimate to work with \(3\)-dicritical digraphs.

---

## 3. A digon-forest theorem

### Theorem 3.1
Let \(D\) be \(3\)-dicritical. Then exactly one of the following holds:

1. \(D\) is a symmetric odd cycle;
2. \(B(D)\) is a forest.

### Proof

If \(B(D)\) is non-bipartite, it contains an odd cycle \(C\). The subdigraph \(\overleftrightarrow C\) has dichromatic number \(3\). By the criticality of \(D\), this subdigraph cannot be proper. Hence \(D=\overleftrightarrow C\).

It remains to exclude cycles in \(B(D)\) when \(B(D)\) is bipartite. Suppose \(xy\) lies on a cycle of \(B(D)\), and delete the arc \(xy\), retaining \(yx\). By criticality, \(D-xy\) has a 2-dicoloring \(c\).

All edges of \(B(D)-xy\) are digons and hence have differently colored endpoints. The alternate \(x\)-to-\(y\) path around the even cycle has odd length, so it forces

\[
c(x)\ne c(y).
\]

Restoring the arc \(xy\) cannot create a monochromatic directed cycle, since its endpoints have different colors. Thus \(c\) would also be a 2-dicoloring of \(D\), a contradiction.

Therefore the bipartite graph \(B(D)\) is acyclic. ∎

### Corollary 3.2
Conjecture 9.2 holds for every critical 2-extremal digraph whose digon graph contains a cycle.

Indeed, Theorem 3.1 forces it to be a symmetric odd cycle, one of the defining members of \(\mathcal H_2\).

This also shows that every non-base counterexample must have a forest as its digon graph.

---

## 4. Complete description when the digon graph is connected

The connected-forest case has a particularly rigid normal form.

### Definition
Let \(T\) be a tree with bipartition \((X,Y)\). Let \(S\subseteq X\), with \(|S|\ge3\), and let

\[
C=s_1s_2\cdots s_qs_1
\]

be a directed cycle whose vertex set is \(S\). Define

\[
D(T,S,C)=\overleftrightarrow T\cup C.
\]

### Theorem 4.1
A \(3\)-dicritical digraph \(D\) with connected digon graph is exactly one of:

1. a symmetric odd cycle; or
2. a digraph \(D(T,S,C)\), where every leaf of \(T\) belongs to \(S\).

### Proof

Assume \(D\) is not a symmetric odd cycle. By Theorem 3.1, its connected digon graph is a tree \(T\), with bipartition \((X,Y)\).

Any 2-dicoloring of \(D\) must properly 2-color all digons. Since \(T\) is connected, this forces the bipartition coloring, up to exchanging colors. Because \(D\) is not 2-dicolorable, one of \(D[X]\) and \(D[Y]\) contains a directed cycle. After exchanging \(X,Y\), let \(C\subseteq D[X]\) be such a cycle, and put \(S=V(C)\).

If \(a\) is any arc outside \(\overleftrightarrow T\cup C\), then \(D-a\) still contains all the digons of \(T\) and the directed cycle \(C\). Its only possible proper coloring of the digons makes \(C\) monochromatic. Thus \(D-a\) is still not 2-dicolorable, contradicting criticality. Therefore

\[
D=\overleftrightarrow T\cup C.
\]

Finally, suppose that a leaf \(v\) of \(T\) does not belong to \(C\). Then \(T-v\) remains connected and still contains \(C\). Consequently \(D-v\) is not 2-dicolorable, again contradicting criticality. Hence every leaf belongs to \(S\subseteq X\).

Conversely, suppose \(D=D(T,S,C)\) and every leaf of \(T\) lies in \(S\).

The digons force all of \(X\) to have one color and all of \(Y\) the other, so \(C\) is monochromatic. Hence \(\vec\chi(D)\ge3\). A 3-dicoloring is obtained by coloring \(Y\) with color 1, \(X-\{s\}\) with color 2, and one \(s\in S\) with color 3. Thus \(\vec\chi(D)=3\).

It remains to check criticality.

- If an arc of \(C\) is deleted, the bipartition coloring of \(T\) is a dicoloring, since \(C\) becomes a directed path.
- Let one direction of a tree edge \(e\) be deleted. The two components of \(T-e\) each contain a leaf, hence each contains a vertex of \(S\). Use the bipartition coloring on one component and its reversal on the other. The vertices of \(S\) then use both colors, so \(C\) is not monochromatic. Every intact digon is bichromatic. The single remaining orientation of \(e\) may be monochromatic, but one endpoint has no other monochromatic tree arc, so it cannot lie on a monochromatic directed cycle.

Thus deleting any arc makes the digraph 2-dicolorable, and every proper subdigraph is 2-dicolorable. ∎

---

## 5. Exact local-connectivity criterion for the tree normal form

Not every \(D(T,S,C)\) from Theorem 4.1 has \(\lambda=2\). The cyclic order of \(S\) matters.

For \(v\in V(T)\), define

\[
q(v)=d_T(v)+\mathbf 1_{v\in S}.
\]

This is both the indegree and the outdegree of \(v\) in \(D(T,S,C)\). Call \(v\) **heavy** if \(q(v)\ge3\).

For an edge \(e\in E(T)\), deleting \(e\) splits \(T\) into two components. Call \(e\) **good** if the vertices of \(S\) in either component form a nonempty proper cyclic interval in the cyclic order given by \(C\). The definition is symmetric, since the complement of a cyclic interval is a cyclic interval.

### Theorem 5.1
For \(D=D(T,S,C)\) as in Theorem 4.1,

\[
\lambda(D)=2
\]

if and only if every two distinct heavy vertices are separated in \(T\) by a good edge. Equivalently, every component obtained by deleting all good edges contains at most one heavy vertex.

### Proof

For \(Z\subset V(D)\), let \(\delta_T(Z)\) be the set of tree edges with one endpoint in \(Z\), and let \(\rho_C(Z)\) be the number of arcs of \(C\) leaving \(Z\). Since every tree edge is a digon,

\[
d_D^+(Z)=|\delta_T(Z)|+\rho_C(Z). \tag{1}
\]

If \(Z\) is nonempty and proper, then \(d_D^+(Z)\ge2\). Indeed:

- If \(|\delta_T(Z)|\ge2\), this is immediate.
- If \(|\delta_T(Z)|=1\), then \(Z\) and its complement are the two sides of a tree edge. Each side contains a leaf of \(T\), hence a vertex of \(S\). Therefore at least one arc of \(C\) leaves \(Z\).

Thus \(D\) is 2-arc-strong.

By (1), a directed cut has size exactly two only in the following cases:

1. \(|\delta_T(Z)|=1\) and \(\rho_C(Z)=1\). This is precisely a side of a good edge.
2. \(|\delta_T(Z)|=2\) and \(\rho_C(Z)=0\). In this case one side contains no vertex of \(S\).

In the second case, the \(S\)-free side contains only vertices of tree degree two. To see this, it is connected—otherwise each component, containing no leaf of \(T\), would contribute at least two boundary edges—and if this side is \(W\), then

\[
\sum_{w\in W}d_T(w)=2(|W|-1)+2=2|W|.
\]

No \(w\in W\) is a leaf, so every term \(d_T(w)\ge2\), and consequently every \(d_T(w)=2\). Such a cut cannot separate two heavy vertices.

If one endpoint of an ordered pair \(u,v\) is not heavy, then either \(d^+(u)\le2\) or \(d^-(v)\le2\), according to the order, and hence \(\lambda_D(u,v)\le2\).

For two heavy vertices \(u,v\), a directed cut of size two separates them exactly when some good edge lies on the unique \(u\)-\(v\) path in \(T\). Directed Menger therefore gives:

- \(\lambda_D(u,v)=2\) if a good edge separates them;
- \(\lambda_D(u,v)\ge3\) otherwise.

The result follows. ∎

### Examples

1. If \(T=K_{1,r}\), \(S\) is its set of leaves, and \(C\) is a directed cycle through the leaves, only the center is heavy. The condition is vacuous, so these directed wheel-like digraphs are 2-extremal.

2. Let \(T\) consist of two degree-three vertices \(y_1,y_2\), joined through a degree-two vertex, with leaves \(a,b\) at \(y_1\) and \(c,d\) at \(y_2\). If

\[
C=a\,c\,b\,d\,a,
\]

then there are three arc-disjoint \(y_1\)-to-\(y_2\) paths:

\[
y_1Ty_2,\qquad y_1ac y_2,\qquad y_1bd y_2.
\]

Thus this \(3\)-dicritical digraph is not 2-extremal. If instead the cyclic order is \(a,b,c,d\), the relevant tree separation is a cyclic interval, and Theorem 5.1 gives \(\lambda=2\).

---

## 6. Exact formulation of the remaining disconnected-forest case

Suppose \(D\) is a non-base critical 2-extremal digraph. By Theorem 3.1,

\[
B(D)=T_1\cup\cdots\cup T_r
\]

is a forest. Choose a bipartition function

\[
\pi_i:V(T_i)\longrightarrow\{0,1\}.
\]

Every 2-coloring avoiding monochromatic digons is uniquely of the form

\[
c(v)=z_i\oplus\pi_i(v),\qquad v\in V(T_i),
\]

for a vector \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_r)\in\{0,1\}^r\).

A directed cycle \(C\) can be monochromatic only if, for every \(i\), the value of \(\pi_i\) is constant on \(V(C)\cap V(T_i)\). Call such a cycle **parity-compatible**. If its support is

\[
I(C)=\{i:V(C)\cap V(T_i)\ne\varnothing\},
\]

and the common parity in \(T_i\) is \(p_i(C)\), then \(C\) is monochromatic exactly when

\[
\{z_i\oplus p_i(C):i\in I(C)\}
\]

has only one value. Consequently, \(D\) is 2-dicolorable if and only if the Boolean variables \(z_i\) satisfy all the NAE constraints

\[
\operatorname{NAE}\bigl(z_i\oplus p_i(C):i\in I(C)\bigr)
\]

over parity-compatible directed cycles \(C\).

For \(r=1\), one such cycle is inevitably monochromatic, and criticality gives the normal form of Theorem 4.1. For \(r\ge2\), different tree components may be flipped independently, and the obstruction becomes a genuinely global minimally unsatisfiable NAE system. Directed Hajós joins naturally produce precisely this disconnected-forest situation.

This is where the present argument stops. I have not proved that every minimally unsatisfiable cycle system allowed by \(\lambda(D)=2\) decomposes into directed Hajós joins and 2-Hajós tree joins, nor found a system yielding a counterexample.

## 7. Conclusion

The following are established:

- A non-base critical 2-extremal digraph has an acyclic digon graph.
- Therefore Conjecture 9.2 is true whenever the digon graph contains a cycle.
- If the digon graph is connected, the digraph has an explicit tree-plus-directed-cycle form.
- Within that form, Theorem 5.1 gives a complete and elementary characterization of when \(\lambda=2\).

The unresolved part is the decomposition of critical digraphs whose digon graph is a disconnected forest. No full proof or counterexample is obtained.
